I was surprised by a very frustrating customer experience with Best Buy. So
I'm at a mall right now waiting for my kids English class to finish. Decided
to buy electronics on Best Buy's website to avoid the crowd. When I was about
to submit my order, my mac turned off. So I go to Best Buy and say: I started
a transaction at your online store, but my mac is out of charge, please lend
me a charger to finish my transaction. The employee says: I cannot let you
borrow a charger, we need them on the tables. I say: "Sorry, maybe I wasn't
clear. I need to finish a transaction on your website. You are an electronics
store, you sell macs, you have a charger, let me finish the transaction,
please." He says, sorry, cannot help you. So I go to an Apple store in another
mall, ask for exactly the same and (miracle!) they are able to lend me a
charger from one of the macs they showcase on a table to finish my transaction
with Best Buy. The moral of the story: Apple loves customers. Best Buy wants
to get rid of them.

How does the amount of data effect accuracy of models? The Accuracy & F1 score
increases as the number of observations increase (see the steep rise in
accuracy and F1). After some increase, they plateau pretty quickly. In this
specific case of a churn model, we see plateau at 5000 data points. This is
just an example. However, the fact that the number is just 5000 means that you
can potentially take a sample of your 'big data' and still arrive at similar
results. Thoughts?

How do you evaluate the technical expertise of someone in a field you are
clueless about? Thus, if you need to hire a data scientist, and you don't know
enough about AI /ML, how do you select the right candidate? The trick is to
find someone who can explain complicated concepts in simple terms. Only a
really confident expert, whose basics are sound, can do this. If he needs to
use jargon, this is a red flag.
